case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that the State's burden at a dispositional hearing on whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised is preponderance of the evidence, and that proof of a single incident resulting in serious bodily injury to the child suffices to support a no-appropriate-treatment-plan finding without proof that the parent caused the injury.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Colorado authority on when a court must adopt a treatment plan and when it may find that none can be devised.
key_cases.quote: we conclude the district court erred by imposing a clear and convincing burden of proof on the state at the dispositional hearing.

key_cases.holding: The division held that a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations for a parent's disability in deciding whether the treatment plan was appropriate and whether the department made reasonable efforts to rehabilitate the parent, and affirmed because the court had done so.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Colorado rule that a court-ordered treatment plan is appropriate only if it accounts for reasonable accommodations for the parent's disability.
key_cases.quote: a juvenile court must consider reasonable accommodations in deciding whether such a parent's treatment plan was appropriate and whether reasonable efforts were made to rehabilitate the parent.

key_cases.holding: As a matter of first impression the division held that the Americans with Disabilities Act does not pre-empt section 19-3-604(1)(b)(I), because the question whether reasonable accommodations could address a parent's mental impairment is subsumed within the statutory question whether an appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the relationship between the ADA accommodation duty and the court's determination that no appropriate treatment plan can be devised.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that it does not conflict with the ADA's requirement that a public entity make reasonable accommodations for qualified individuals with disabilities.

key_cases.holding: The court held that consideration of less drastic alternatives is implicit in the statutory termination criteria, that due process does not require express findings on them, and that the child's best interests rather than an 'adequacy' standard control; it reversed the court of appeals for substituting its judgment for the trial court's.
key_cases.relevance: The court restates the four statutory findings, including non-compliance with or failure of an appropriate court-approved treatment plan, that a service order must be measured against.
key_cases.quote: Implicit in these criteria is the requirement that the trial court consider and eliminate less drastic alternatives.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination, holding that a trial court's consideration and elimination of alternatives less drastic than termination is implicit in the statutory termination criteria, so that no separate express finding is required, and that a treatment plan's appropriateness is measured against the realities that produced the dependency adjudication rather than by whether it ultimately succeeded.
key_cases.relevance: This is the foundational Colorado holding on what makes a court-ordered treatment plan appropriate — a plan reasonably calculated to render this parent fit within a reasonable time, measured against the conditions that caused the adjudication — and it is the source A.M., 2021 CO 14, cites for the less-drastic-alternatives rule.
key_cases.quote: adherence to the statutory criteria for termination requires a trial court to consider less drastic alternatives and to reject those alternatives as unavailing before entering an order of termination

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination of the mother's parental rights, holding that ample evidence supported the district court's findings under the section 19-3-604(1)(c) criteria — failure of an appropriate treatment plan, unfitness, and conduct unlikely to change within a reasonable time — and restating that a court ruling on a termination motion must give primary consideration to the child's physical, mental and emotional conditions and needs.
key_cases.relevance: This is the current Colorado Supreme Court statement of the section 19-3-604(1)(c) criteria against which a court-ordered treatment plan is measured, including the expedited-permanency rule that a parent who exhibits the same problems without adequate improvement cannot be found in reasonable compliance.
key_cases.quote: In considering a motion to terminate the parent-child legal relationship, the court shall give primary consideration to the physical, mental, and emotional conditions and needs of the child.

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives
